edges.rationale: The two control approaches are solutions to the congestion problem; understanding what congestion is and its costs (queuing delay, loss, collapse) is needed before classifying how to control it.
Classic TCP infers congestion from packet loss and growing delay; learners must first know that loss and queuing delay are the symptoms and costs of congestion that TCP reacts to.

Classic TCP is the canonical instance of end-to-end control (inferring congestion from loss/delay because IP provides no explicit feedback); the taxonomy is required to frame why TCP works the way it does.

edges.dependent: Newer TCP Variants: Delay-Based and ECN
edges.rationale: The newer variants are organized by this taxonomy: delay-based TCP is still end-to-end inference (via delay), while ECN is network-assisted explicit feedback; the approach distinction is needed to classify them.
The fairness analysis examines how AIMD's additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease converges to equal bandwidth shares with a sawtooth pattern; AIMD must be understood first.

edges.dependent: Newer TCP Variants: Delay-Based and ECN
edges.rationale: The newer variants are presented as alternatives that determine the sending rate more quickly than classic loss-based TCP; the classic mechanisms (slow start, AIMD, loss-triggered reaction) are the baseline being contrasted.

edges.dependent: Impact of Slow Start on Latency
edges.rationale: Analyzing how slow start contributes to end-to-end delay requires first understanding the slow-start mechanism itself, which is part of classic TCP congestion control.

edges.prerequisite: Impact of Slow Start on Latency
edges.dependent: Newer TCP Variants: Delay-Based and ECN
edges.rationale: The latency analysis of slow start explicitly motivates designs that determine the sending rate more quickly, which is exactly what the delay-based and ECN variants do.
